rows.verified: Optical radiation includes ultraviolet, visible and infrared radiation.
The Control of Artificial Optical Radiation at Work Regulations protect workers from hazardous artificial optical radiation.
Businesses using hazardous artificial optical-radiation sources must reduce associated risks as low as reasonably practicable.
High-power lasers can cause serious eye damage, blindness and skin burns.
Embedded lasers in office equipment are not a risk while protective housings remain undamaged.
Only trained and authorised people should perform maintenance that gives access to embedded lasers.
Protective eyewear requirements depend on the employer's risk assessment and the laser class and access conditions.
HSE encourages employers of outdoor workers to include sun-protection advice in routine health and safety training.
Optical-radiation controls depend on wavelength, power, exposure duration, beam access, equipment condition and work practice.
Optical-radiation evidence is equipment- and exposure-specific and is not an exact parcel-level health probability.
A biological agent is a micro-organism or other agent that may cause infection, allergy, toxicity or another hazard to human health.
Biological agents at work can include bacteria, fungi, viruses, parasites and agents associated with transmissible spongiform encephalopathies.
Some biological agents are zoonotic and may pass from animals to humans.
Employers must consider both deliberate work with biological agents and incidental exposure arising from work activities.
Workers can be at risk of infection when biological hazards are not adequately controlled.
Information and training should explain infection risks and the controls workers must follow.
Suitable hygiene, containment, cleaning and exposure-control arrangements should reflect the biological hazard and work activity.
Pregnancy can increase the significance of some workplace infection risks and should be considered in risk management.
Biological-agent controls depend on the organism, route of exposure, activity, concentration, containment and susceptible workers.
Biological-hazard evidence is organism- and activity-specific and is not an exact parcel-level infection probability.
